question: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.
steps: Look at each picture and spot the circles in it.
Sketch the circles in the right places and sizes.
Compare your freehand circles with the pictures and see how round they are.
figure: Five circle artworks: two equal touching circles; two concentric circles (inner about half the outer); three equal overlapping circles in a row; mouse face made of circles (big face, two ear circles, two eye circles, dot nose, line mouth); X made of two crossing lines with a small circle at each lower end.

question: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
answer: All the points you mark lie on a round curve around P, each exactly 4 cm from P. With enough points they join into a circle of radius 4 cm.
steps: Mark P in the middle of the page.
Place the ruler with 0 cm at P and mark a point at 4 cm.
Turn the ruler to another direction and mark another point at 4 cm from P; repeat in many directions.
Notice the points form a round shape around P.
figure: Point P with dashed segments to Q and R, each labelled 4 cm, in different directions.

question: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the point P. How would they look?
answer: They would form a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.
steps: Every point is the same distance, 4 cm, from P.
Joining all such points gives a perfectly round curve.
This curve is a circle with centre P.

question: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.
steps: Place the compass next to a ruler and open it until the tip and the pencil point are 4 cm apart.
Put the tip firmly on P.
Keep the tip fixed and move only the pencil all the way round.
figure: Compass opened against a ruler (tip at 4 on the scale) and a circle drawn with centre P and a radius marked.

question: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?
answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.
steps: The pencil stayed exactly 4 cm from the tip all the time.
So every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
This fixed distance is the radius; P is the centre.

question: Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.
answer: Open ended. Correct drawings: touching circles have centres at a distance of twice the radius; concentric circles share one centre but have different radii; overlapping circles have centres closer than twice the radius; the mouse face has all its circles drawn with a compass.
steps: Choose a radius and set the compass with the ruler.
Fix the tip at each centre and draw each circle.
For concentric circles, keep the same tip point and change the radius.
Add the dots and lines with a ruler.

question: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?
answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.
steps: Draw the head circle with the compass.
Draw the neck as a short vertical line below the circle.
Draw the body as a rectangle without the top edge: two vertical sides and a flat bottom.
Fix a radius and try the tip at different spots above the body until the arc from one top corner to the other touches the bottom of the neck line.
Draw the arc and rub out the trial marks.
figure: A circle (head) with a short vertical line below it reaching the middle of a curved top edge of a rectangle (body). The top edge is a downward dipping arc joining the two top corners; sides vertical and bottom flat.
note: No measurements given in the book.

question: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The first wave is a half circle on the left half of AB lying above the line (A to X), and the second wave is a half circle on the right half lying below the line (X to B). Both half circles are shaded with vertical lines.
answer: AB = 8 cm, AX = XB = 4 cm. Each half circle has diameter 4 cm, so radius 2 cm. First half circle: tip at the point 2 cm from A on AB, drawn above the line. Second half circle: tip at the point 6 cm from A on AB, drawn below the line.
steps: Draw AB = 8 cm with a ruler.
Mark X on AB at 4 cm from A.
Set the compass to 2 cm; put the tip at the point 2 cm from A and draw a half circle above AB from A to X.
Put the tip at the point 6 cm from A (2 cm from B) and draw a half circle below AB from X to B.
Shade both half circles with vertical lines.
figure: Horizontal line AB = 8 cm. A semicircle above AB from A to point X (AX marked with a question mark), then a second semicircle below the line from X to B. Both semicircles shaded with vertical lines.

question: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points A and B) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.
steps: Draw two light horizontal guide lines (supporting lines) that help to place the compass tips.
Choose a radius and place the tip at B to draw the upper curve between the two corners.
Place the tip at A, the same distance from the middle on the other side, and with the same radius draw the lower curve.
Fill the pupil circle in the middle.
Repeat for the second eye and adjust until both eyes are symmetrical and identical.
figure: Two identical almond shaped eyes side by side, each with a filled black circle in the centre.
note: Book gives a hint at the end of the chapter, no lengths.

question: In the wave with a central line AB = 8 cm, the first wave is a half circle from A to X on the line AB. What radius should be taken in the compass to get this half circle? What should be the length of AX?

parts.label: a
parts.question: What radius should be taken in the compass?

parts.label: b
parts.question: What should be the length of AX?

answer: a) 2 cm, b) AX = 4 cm
steps: The two equal half circles share the 8 cm line, so AX is 8 cm divided by 2, which gives 4 cm.
AX is the diameter of the half circle.
Radius = 4 cm ÷ 2 = 2 cm.
figure: Line AB of 8 cm; half circle above it from A to X; compass radius and AX marked with question marks.

question: Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.
answer: Open ended. For a central line of length L, each half circle has diameter L ÷ 2 and radius L ÷ 4. Example: L = 10 cm gives two half circles of diameter 5 cm and radius 2.5 cm; L = 12 cm gives radius 3 cm.
steps: Draw a line AB of any length L.
Mark the middle point X.
Set the compass to L ÷ 4 and draw the first half circle above AB from A to X.
Draw the second half circle below AB from X to B with the same radius.

book_label: Figure it Out Q3, Try This (section 8.1)
question: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half circle (as appearing in the neck of the figure 'A Person'). The challenge here is to get both the waves to be identical. This may be tricky!
answer: Open ended. Both waves are arcs of the same radius on the same length of chord. A correct drawing shows two identical arcs, one above the line and one below the line, each shorter than a half circle.
steps: Draw the central line and mark the chord for each wave.
Choose one radius bigger than half the chord.
For the upper arc, place the tip below the line on the perpendicular through the middle of the chord, at a fixed distance, and draw the arc above the line.
For the lower arc, place the tip above the line at the same distance from the line and use the same radius.
Check that both arcs look identical.
figure: Waves like the neck of A Person: arcs smaller than a half circle, one above and one below the central line.

question: What shapes are a rectangle and four small squares drawn in a group? What makes them squares and rectangles?
answer: A rectangle has two properties: R1) its opposite sides are equal in length, and R2) all its angles are 90°. A square has: S1) all its sides are equal, and S2) all its angles are 90°.
steps: Look at a rectangle: its opposite sides are equal and each corner is a right angle.
Look at a square: all four sides are equal and each corner is a right angle.
figure: A rectangle in the middle (about twice as wide as tall) with four small squares around it, one near each corner.

question: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). Besides ABCD it can be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. Can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? What names are allowed and what names are not?
answer: No. ABDC and ACBD are not allowed. In a valid name the corners come in order, going round the rectangle, starting from any corner and going in either direction.
steps: Check that each pair of letters next to each other in the name is a side of the rectangle.
ABDC fails because B to D is a diagonal, not a side.
So go round the rectangle one corner after another.
figure: Rectangle ABCD with A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left (sides AB, BC, CD, DA).

question: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The square has corners S (top left), P (top right), Q (bottom right) and R (bottom left). 1. PQSR 2. SPQR 3. RSPQ 4. QRSP

parts.question: PQSR
parts.answer: Not a name (Q to S is a diagonal)

answer: PQSR
steps: Going round the square the corners come in the order S, P, Q, R.
SPQR, RSPQ and QRSP follow this order.
PQSR goes from Q to S, which is a diagonal, so it is not a valid name.
figure: Square with S top left, P top right, R bottom left, Q bottom right.

question: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90°. It is rotated (tilted so it looks like a diamond). Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90°?
answer: Yes, it is still a square. All the sides are still equal and all the angles are still 90°, because rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles. In the same way a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.
steps: Rotating does not change lengths.
Rotating does not change angles.
So both square properties S1 and S2 still hold.
figure: A square with horizontal and vertical sides next to the same square turned so its corners point up, down, left and right. Later a tilted rectangle.

question: Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.
steps: Draw the rectangle on dots, counting dots along each side.
From each corner of the rectangle, move one dot diagonally outwards (same count each time).
Draw an equal square at each of the four places, counting the same number of dots for every square.
Use the same counts on the left and right, top and bottom so the figure is symmetrical.
figure: A rectangle (about 15 dots by 7 dots) with four equal squares (about 4 dots by 4 dots) placed diagonally off its four corners with equal gaps.
note: Dot counts are read from the picture and are approximate.

question: Identify if there are any squares in this collection. Use measurements if needed. On a dot grid there are four tilted 4-sided figures with corners on dots: A is a diamond whose left to right span equals its top to bottom span (about 8 dots each way); B is a diamond about 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall; C is a diamond about 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall; D is a small tilted long rectangle.
answer: A is a square.
steps: A square needs 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°.
A has equal width and height, so its sides and angles are equal: a square.
B and C have unequal widths and heights, so they are diamonds whose angles are not 90°.
D has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.
figure: Four tilted figures on a dot grid labelled A, B, C, D: A a square-shaped diamond, B a narrow tall diamond, C a wide diamond, D a small tilted rectangle.
note: Dot counts are read from the picture and are approximate; the book answer is A only, which agrees with my check.

question: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments in the above figure? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?
answer: Yes. The positions of the dots make it possible. Moving from one corner to the next by the same number of dots across and down, and turning with the counts swapped, gives equal sides and right angles.
steps: Count how many dots across and how many down it takes to go from one corner to the next.
If every side uses the same counts, the sides are equal.
If the next side uses the counts swapped for a turn (across and down exchanged), the angle is 90°.

question: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and 4 angles of 90°. For example a diamond with corners 4 dots up, 4 dots right, 4 dots down and 4 dots left of its centre is a square.
steps: Pick dots as corners so that each side goes the same number of dots across and down for a square.
Join the corners with a ruler.
Measure the sides with the ruler.
Check the angles with a protractor or a set square.

question: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.
answer: Square PQRS with PQ = QR = RS = SP = 6 cm and all angles 90°. RS = 6 cm and ∠R = ∠S = 90°.
steps: Draw PQ = 6 cm with a ruler.
Place the protractor with its centre at P and its baseline along PQ, mark 90° and draw a perpendicular through P.
Mark S on this perpendicular so that PS = 6 cm (ruler), or open the compass to 6 cm, tip at P, and mark an arc.
At Q draw the perpendicular to PQ and mark R with QR = 6 cm (with the compass: keep the radius at 6 cm and put the tip at Q).
Join R and S. Check RS = 6 cm, ∠R = 90°, ∠S = 90°.
figure: Six steps: segment PQ = 6 cm; protractor at P marking a perpendicular; S marked with PS = 6 cm and a 90° mark at P; compass opened to 6 cm; R marked at 6 cm above Q; final square PQRS with 6 cm sides and 90° marks at P and Q.

question: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you see why PS should be 6 cm long?
answer: Because all the sides of a square are equal, so PS must be the same length as PQ, which is 6 cm.
steps: Property S1: all sides of a square are equal.
PQ = 6 cm, so PS = 6 cm.

question: In the square PQRS of side 6 cm just constructed, how long is the side RS and what are the measures of ∠R and ∠S?
steps: All sides of a square are equal, so RS = 6 cm.
All angles of a square are 90°, so ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

question: Draw a rectangle with sides of length 4 cm and 6 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 4 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm and ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90°. Both properties hold.
steps: Draw AB = 4 cm.
Draw perpendiculars at A and B.
Mark D on the one at A with AD = 6 cm and C on the one at B with BC = 6 cm.
Join D and C.
Measure: opposite sides are equal (4 and 4, 6 and 6) and all angles are 90°.
figure: Rectangle ABCD with AB = 4 cm at the bottom and the sides AD and BC 6 cm tall, right angle marks at A and B.

question: Draw a rectangle of sides 2 cm and 10 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 10 cm, PS = QR = 2 cm and ∠P = ∠Q = ∠R = ∠S = 90°.
steps: Draw PQ = 10 cm.
Draw perpendiculars at P and Q.
Mark S with PS = 2 cm and R with QR = 2 cm.
Join S and R.
Check that SR = 10 cm and all angles are 90°.
figure: Long thin rectangle PQRS, PQ = 10 cm along the bottom and QR = 2 cm.

question: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal?
answer: No. If all four angles are 90° the figure is a rectangle, so its opposite sides are equal.
steps: Draw one side and the two perpendiculars at its ends.
The two perpendiculars stay the same distance apart, so the opposite side is the same length as the first side.
So opposite sides are always equal.

question: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.
answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 7 cm and BC = AD = 4 cm, all angles 90°.
steps: Draw AB = 7 cm.
Draw a perpendicular at A and mark D with AD = 4 cm.
Draw a perpendicular at B and mark C with BC = 4 cm.
Join D and C and check DC = 7 cm.
figure: Four copies of rectangle ABCD (AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm) with X on AD and Y on BC joined by a dashed line. Case 1: X is 5 mm from A and Y is 1 cm from C. Case 2: X is 1 cm from A and Y is 2 cm from B. Case 3: X = D and Y = B, XY is the diagonal. Case 4: X = A and Y = B, XY = AB.

question: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
answer: Closest: when X and Y are the same distance from A and B respectively (for example X = A and Y = B), where XY = 7 cm. Farthest: when X is at one corner and Y at the opposite corner (X = A and Y = C, or X = D and Y = B), where XY is a diagonal of about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).
steps: Try several positions with a ruler.
XY is 7 cm whenever X and Y are at equal distances from A and B.
XY is longest when X and Y are at opposite corners.

question: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB (7 cm)?
answer: The minimum distance of XY is 7 cm, which is equal to AB.
steps: Measure XY when X and Y are level (same distance from A and B).
You get 7 cm each time, which is the length of AB.

question: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill in: When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm.

parts.label: a
parts.question: X is 5 mm from A and Y is 3 cm from B

parts.label: b
parts.question: X is 1 cm from A and Y is 1 cm from B

parts.label: c
parts.question: X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B

answer: a) 7 cm 4 mm, b) 7 cm 0 mm, c) 7 cm 3 mm
steps: Across the rectangle the distance is 7 cm; the up and down difference between the two points changes.
a) the difference is 3 cm − 5 mm = 2.5 cm, XY = √(49 + 6.25) ≈ 7.4 cm.
b) the difference is 0, XY = 7 cm.
c) the difference is 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm, XY = √(49 + 4) ≈ 7.3 cm.
note: Book answers agree with my check: 7.43 cm, 7.00 cm, 7.28 cm (to the nearest mm). In the figure for case 2 the book marks Y as 2 cm from B, which differs from the bullet text (1 cm from B).

question: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as a table with columns: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY. Fill the table for the three cases above.

parts.question: X from A: 5 mm, Y from B: 3 cm
X from A: 1 cm, Y from B: 1 cm
X from A: 2 cm, Y from B: 4 cm

answer: Rows: (5 mm, 3 cm, 7.4 cm), (1 cm, 1 cm, 7 cm), (2 cm, 4 cm, 7.3 cm).
steps: Write each case as a row.
Put the two distances and then the measured length XY.
figure: Empty table with three columns and three rows.

question: What happens to the length XY when X and Y are placed at the same distance away from A and B, respectively? Fill the table: X from A is 5 mm and Y from B is 5 mm; X from A is 1 cm and Y from B is 1 cm; X from A is 1 cm 5 mm and Y from B is 1 cm 5 mm.
answer: XY = 7 cm in every case, the same as AB.
steps: Equal distances mean X and Y are at the same height.
So XY is parallel to AB and as long as AB: 7 cm.
note: The printed solution page copies the question table with Y distances 5 cm, 1 cm, 4 cm, but the chapter itself has 5 mm, 1 cm, 1 cm 5 mm. The answer 7 cm holds for equal distances.

question: In each of these cases (X and Y at the same distance from A and B), observe 1. how the length XY compares to that of AB and 2. the shape of the 4-sided figure ABYX.
answer: XY = AB; ABYX is a rectangle.
steps: XY and AB are both 7 cm.
The four angles at A, B, Y and X are all 90° and opposite sides are equal, so ABYX is a rectangle.

question: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of AC? BD? (AC and BD are the diagonals of rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.)
answer: The farthest distance between X and Y is equal to AC or BD, which is about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).
steps: The farthest is when X and Y are at opposite corners.
Then XY is exactly a diagonal, AC or BD.
note: Book says equal to AC or BD; for 7 cm by 4 cm, √65 ≈ 8.06 cm (my computation).

question: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares (a rectangle split by two vertical lines into three equal squares).
answer: Any rectangle whose length is 3 times its breadth, for example 9 cm by 3 cm. Each square has side 3 cm.
steps: Choose the square side, say 3 cm.
Draw a rough diagram showing 3 equal squares side by side.
Draw AB = 3 cm, draw perpendiculars at A and B, and mark AD = 3 cm and BC = 3 cm.
Use the compass to transfer the 3 cm length along the line two more times so that the total length is 9 cm.
Draw the dividing lines to check each part is a 3 cm square.
figure: A rectangle divided by two vertical lines into three equal squares.

book_label: Explore: rectangle divided into two identical squares (section 8.4)
question: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two identical squares ABEF and BCDE, with no measurements imposed. If AF is assigned 4 cm, what must the length of AC be?
answer: AC = 8 cm. The rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm.
steps: Draw a rough diagram: AB = BC and FE = ED, and all the short lines are equal (AF = AB = BE = FE = BC = CD = ED).
Draw AF = 4 cm.
Draw a line perpendicular to AF at A. With the compass tip at A and radius AF, mark B on this line.
Keep the same radius and mark C beyond B so that BC = AF.
Do the same at F to place the other corners and complete the rectangle ACDF.
figure: Rough figure: rectangle ACDF (top A, B, C; bottom F, E, D) with B and E joined, making two squares ABEF and BCDE with tick marks on equal sides.
note: Book does not print the value of AC; computed: 4 cm + 4 cm = 8 cm.

question: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be divided into two identical squares, and of a rectangle that cannot be divided into three identical squares.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Cannot be divided into two identical squares
parts.answer: Length 4 cm, breadth 2.5 cm (many answers possible)

parts.label: b
parts.question: Cannot be divided into three identical squares
parts.answer: Length 7 cm, breadth 2 cm (many answers possible)

answer: a) for example 4 cm by 2.5 cm, b) for example 7 cm by 2 cm (other answers possible)
steps: A rectangle splits into two identical squares only if length = 2 × breadth.
4 cm is not 2 × 2.5 cm.
It splits into three only if length = 3 × breadth; 7 cm is not 3 × 2 cm.

book_label: Construct 1: A Square within a Rectangle (section 8.4)
question: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm. How will you construct a square inside, as shown in the figure, such that the centre of the square is the same as the centre of the rectangle? (The square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle and sits in the middle of its length.)
answer: The square has side 4 cm. Its left and right sides are 2 cm away from the left and right sides of the rectangle.
steps: Draw the 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
The square must fit between top and bottom, so its side is 4 cm.
Leave (8 cm − 4 cm) ÷ 2 = 2 cm on each side.
Mark points 2 cm in from each short side and draw the vertical lines of the square.
figure: Rectangle 8 cm wide and 4 cm tall with two vertical lines creating a middle square.
note: Book hint: draw a rough figure; what is the sidelength of the square and the distance between corners of the square and outer rectangle. No printed solution; computed from the figure.

question: Construct three squares of side 4 cm placed in a staircase, each touching the next at one corner (the top right corner of a lower square touches the bottom left corner of the square above it). Now try with squares of side 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm placed in the same way, with the 7 cm square at the bottom left and the 3 cm square at the top right.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: three 4 cm squares meeting corner to corner, and then squares of sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm meeting corner to corner in a staircase.
steps: Draw the first square of side 4 cm with perpendicular sides.
From its top right corner draw the next square of side 4 cm going up and right.
Repeat for the third.
For the second picture start with 7 cm, then 5 cm, then 3 cm.
figure: Staircase of three 4 cm squares touching at corners; and a staircase of squares 7 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm from bottom to top, touching at corners.

question: Construct the figure: a large square divided into smaller squares, some halved by diagonals with one half shaded with parallel lines, and a plain larger square in a corner. Choose measurements of your choice. The larger 4-sided figure is a square and so are the smaller ones.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing has a large square made of equal small squares (with one plain larger square covering a 2 by 2 block), with diagonals drawn and the same triangle of each small square shaded.
steps: Choose the side of the small square, say 1 cm, and draw the large square of 4 cm by 4 cm.
Draw the grid lines using perpendiculars.
Draw the diagonals in the small squares.
Shade one triangle in each with parallel lines.
figure: A square split into a 4 by 4 grid of small squares; most small squares have a diagonal with one triangle hatched; the bottom left 2 by 2 block is one plain larger square.

question: Construct a square with a circular hole whose centre is the same as the centre of the square.
answer: The centre of the circle should be at the meeting point of the two diagonals of the square (the line segments joining opposite corners).
steps: Draw the square.
Draw both diagonals; they meet at the centre.
Put the compass tip at that point and draw a circle inside the square.
figure: A square with a smaller circle in its middle.

question: Construct a large square divided into 4 equal smaller squares (2 by 2) with a circular hole in the centre of each small square.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing has four equal squares, each with a circle of the same radius at its centre (the meeting point of its diagonals).
steps: Draw one square and its middle lines to form 4 equal squares.
Draw the diagonals of each small square to find its centre.
Draw a circle with the same radius at each centre.
figure: A square divided into four equal squares, each with a circle at its centre.

book_label: Construct 6: Square with Curves, Try This (section 8.4)
question: This is a square with 8 cm sidelengths. Construct it so that four arcs, one on each side, bulge uniformly inwards from each side, each arc going from one corner of its side to the other corner.
answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: a square of side 8 cm with four equal arcs bulging inward. For example, use radius 8 cm and place each compass tip outside the square at the point that is 8 cm from both ends of that side; each arc then dips about 1 cm into the square.
steps: Draw a square of side 8 cm.
Open the compass to 8 cm.
Put the tip at one end of a side and mark an arc outside the square; do the same from the other end; the two arcs cross at a point outside.
Put the tip at that crossing point and draw the arc from one corner to the other.
Repeat for the other three sides.
figure: A square with four arcs, each joining two neighbouring corners and curving inward, forming a four pointed star shape inside.
note: Book gives only a hint (where to place the compass tip so that the 4 arcs bulge uniformly). The 8 cm radius is my example choice.

question: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS. Predict whether the two diagonals are equal in length, then construct a rectangle (for example 6 cm by 4 cm) and measure both diagonals. What do you find?
answer: The two diagonals are equal in length. For a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle each diagonal is about 7.2 cm.
steps: Draw a rectangle PQRS, for example 6 cm long and 4 cm wide, using the ruler and set square or compass.
Join P to R and Q to S.
Measure PR and QS with the ruler.
Both measure about 7.2 cm, so the diagonals are equal.
Try another rectangle: the diagonals are equal again.
figure: Rectangle PQRS (P top-left, Q top-right, R bottom-right, S bottom-left) with both diagonals PR and QS drawn.
note: Book gives no printed answer. Check: diagonal of 6 by 4 rectangle is sqrt(36 + 16) = sqrt(52), about 7.2 cm.

book_label: In text (section 8.5): are g and h equal, are c and d equal
question: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Are g and h equal?
parts.answer: Not in general. They are equal only when the rectangle is a square (each 45°).

parts.label: b
parts.question: Are c and d equal?
parts.answer: Not in general. They are equal only when the rectangle is a square (each 45°).

answer: a) g and h are not equal unless the rectangle is a square; b) c and d are not equal unless the rectangle is a square. In every rectangle g + h = 90° and c + d = 90°.
steps: Draw a rectangle that is not a square, for example 6 cm by 4 cm, and its diagonal PR.
Measure c, d at P and g, h at R with a protractor.
For 6 cm by 4 cm the angles are about 34° and 56°, so c and d differ.
In a square both angles are 45°.
In each case the two small angles add up to 90°.
figure: Rectangle PQRS with diagonal PR; at P the angles c (next to PS) and d (next to PQ); at R the angles g (next to RQ) and h (next to RS).
note: Book gives no printed answer. Check: for a 6 by 4 rectangle the angle between the diagonal and the 6 cm side is arctan(4/6), about 33.7°, and the other is about 56.3°.

book_label: In text (section 8.5): identify pairs of equal angles
question: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
answer: d = e = a = h (the four angles next to the sides PQ and SR) and c = f = g = b (the four angles next to the sides PS and QR). Also c + d = 90°.
steps: Draw a rectangle that is not a square and both its diagonals.
Measure all eight angles with a protractor.
The four angles next to the long sides come out equal: d, e, a, h.
The four angles next to the short sides come out equal: c, f, g, b.
Each pair from the two groups adds up to 90°.
figure: Rectangle PQRS with both diagonals and the eight angles a to h labelled as in the question.
note: Book gives no printed answer. Verified by parallel sides (d = h, c = g, e = a, f = b by alternate angles) and equal diagonals (the diagonals bisect each other, so triangles at the sides are isosceles).

question: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal divides the opposite angles into equal parts?
answer: The two adjacent sides must be equal, that is, the rectangle must be a square. Then each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°.
steps: Try rectangles whose sides are different: the diagonal splits the right angle into unequal parts.
Make the adjacent sides equal, for example 5 cm and 5 cm.
Draw the diagonal and measure: both parts are 45°.
So only a square works.

question: What general laws did you observe with respect to the angles and sides of a rectangle and its diagonals? Try to frame them.
answer: In every rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all angles are 90°; the two diagonals are equal in length (and cut each other into equal halves); each diagonal divides the opposite angles into two angles that add up to 90°; the angles the diagonals make with the sides are equal in pairs (d = e = a = h and c = f = g = b). If the adjacent sides are equal (a square), each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°; if not, the two parts are unequal.
steps: Look at your table of sides and the eight angles for several rectangles.
Notice which numbers repeat in each row.
Write each repeated pattern as a rule.
Check the special case of a square separately.
note: Open discussion in the book; the answer shown is a correct summary of what the measurements show.

book_label: Math Talk (section 8.5): will the laws always be true
question: How can one be sure that the laws you have observed will always be true?
answer: Measuring a few examples cannot prove a law for every rectangle, because measurements are approximate and we cannot try all rectangles. We need a reason that works for any rectangle, such as using what we know (opposite sides equal, all angles 90°, alternate angles at parallel sides) to explain why the pattern must hold.
steps: Try many different rectangles and see if the law holds each time.
Notice that measurements are only close, not exact.
Look for a reason using properties already known, for example that opposite sides are parallel.
A reason that works for every rectangle makes us sure.
note: Open-ended discussion question.

book_label: In text (section 8.5): the case of a square
question: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of the rectangle are equal, that is, a square. Draw a square (for example with side 5 cm), draw both diagonals, and see what happens.
answer: In a square each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. All eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are 45°, and the two diagonals are equal (about 7.1 cm for a 5 cm square).
steps: Draw a square of side 5 cm.
Join both diagonals.
Measure the eight angles with a protractor: each is 45°.
Measure the diagonals: both are about 7.1 cm.
figure: Square PQRS with side 5 cm and both diagonals drawn.
note: Book gives the same fact in the Explore solution. Diagonal check: 5 × sqrt(2), about 7.07 cm.

question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 60° and 30°.
answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 60° with side AB and 30° with side AD (angle A = 90° = 60° + 30°). The side lengths can be chosen freely, as only the angles are given.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular line (90°).
At A use the protractor to draw a 60° angle with AB. Where this ray meets the perpendicular from B, mark C.
Through A draw a line perpendicular to AB. This is the line on which D lies, and angle A is now 60° + 30°.
Find D. Method 1: draw a perpendicular to BC at C, and D is where it meets the line through A. Method 2: with the compass take length BC and mark D on the line through A so that AD = BC.
Join CD. ABCD is the rectangle. Check: AB = CD, AD = BC and every angle is 90°.
figure: Rough diagram: rectangle ABCD (A bottom-left, B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left), diagonal AC, with angle between AC and AB marked 60° and angle between AC and AD marked 30°, right angle at D.

question: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two angles. One measures 60°. Check what the other angle is.
steps: Angle A of a rectangle is 90°.
The two parts add up to 90°.
Check with a protractor: the other angle measures 30°.
figure: Rectangle with vertical line through A, base AB, diagonal AC making 60° with AB.
note: The book's rough diagram shows the 30° angle; consistent.

question: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
answer: Rectangle ABCD with DC = AB = 5 cm and diagonal DB = 7 cm. The other two sides AD = BC come out about 4.9 cm and all four angles are 90°.
steps: Draw base DC = 5 cm.
At C draw a line l perpendicular to DC (90°).
With the compass opened to 7 cm and centre D, draw an arc that cuts line l. The cutting point is B (DB = 7 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to DC at D and a perpendicular to BC at B. They meet at A. (Or mark A with the compass so that DA = CB and AB = DC.)
Check: AB = 5 cm, BC = AD, angles 90°, diagonal DB = 7 cm.
figure: Rough diagram: rectangle ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left); DC = 5 cm along the bottom; diagonal DB = 7 cm.
note: Other side: sqrt(7 × 7 − 5 × 5) = sqrt(24), about 4.9 cm (computed check, not stated in the book).

question: To construct the rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, which line can be drawn first?
answer: The base CD, which is 5 cm long.
steps: Only one length that is a side is known: 5 cm.
Draw this side first as the base CD.
The other points can be found from it.
note: Answer stated in the book text.

question: Line l is perpendicular to DC at C, and the point B must lie on l. What else do we know about the position of B?
answer: B is at a distance of 7 cm from the point D (since the diagonal DB is 7 cm).
steps: The diagonal DB = 7 cm.
So B is 7 cm from D.
B is also on line l.
B is the point of l that is 7 cm from D.
figure: Base DC = 5 cm with a perpendicular line l drawn at C.
note: Answer stated in the book text.

question: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets line l at a point. What is the distance of that point from D?
answer: 7 cm. This point is the required point B.
steps: Every point of a circle is at the radius distance from the centre.
The radius is 7 cm.
So the point where the circle meets l is 7 cm from D, and it is B.
figure: Circle of radius 7 cm centred at D; segment DC = 5 cm and perpendicular line l at C, which cuts the circle.
note: Follows from the definition of a circle; the book leaves it as an observation.

question: In the finished rectangle ABCD (DC = 5 cm, diagonal DB = 7 cm), check that it satisfies R1 (opposite sides are equal in length) and R2 (all the angles are 90°).
answer: Yes. AB = DC = 5 cm and AD = BC (about 4.9 cm each), and all four angles are 90°.
steps: Measure AB and DC with a ruler: both 5 cm.
Measure AD and BC: both about 4.9 cm.
Check each corner with a set square or protractor: 90°.
So R1 and R2 hold.
note: AD = BC = sqrt(24), about 4.9 cm, computed.

question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 50° and 40°.
answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 50° with side AB and 40° with side AD (at C the diagonal makes 50° with CD and 40° with CB). Side lengths are free.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular (90°).
At A draw a 50° angle with AB. The ray meets the perpendicular from B at C.
Draw the perpendicular to AB at A. Then the other angle at A is 90° − 50° = 40°.
Draw a perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
Check: AB = CD, AD = BC, all angles 90°.
figure: Rectangle ABCD, AB along the bottom (arbitrary length), diagonal AC; 50° at A next to AB and 40° at A next to AD; at C, 50° next to CD and 40° next to CB.
note: These Construct tasks are the exercise block of section 8.5; ids use FiO form for consistency. Book solution agrees with 90° − 50° = 40°.

question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. What do you observe about the sides?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Construct the rectangle.
parts.answer: Rectangle ABCD with the diagonal AC making 45° with both AB and AD.

parts.label: b
parts.question: What do you observe about the sides?
parts.answer: All four sides are equal, so the rectangle is a square.

answer: a) the rectangle is built with 45° at A next to AB and 45° next to AD; b) all the sides are equal, so it is a square.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular.
At A draw a 45° angle with AB. It meets the perpendicular at C.
Draw the perpendicular to AB at A (the other angle at A is 90° − 45° = 45°).
Draw the perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
Measure the sides: AB = BC = CD = DA. It is a square.
figure: Square ABCD with diagonal AC; 45° and 45° at A and at C; tick marks show all four sides equal.
note: Agrees with the Explore answer (diagonal divides equally only for a square).

question: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 4 cm and the diagonal is of length 8 cm.
answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 4 cm and diagonal QS = 8 cm. The other sides PS = QR are about 6.9 cm.
steps: Draw PQ = 4 cm.
At P draw a perpendicular line.
With the compass opened to 8 cm and centre Q, draw an arc cutting this perpendicular at S (QS = 8 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to PQ at Q and a line through S parallel to PQ (perpendicular to PS). They meet at R.
Check: PQ = SR = 4 cm, PS = QR, angles 90°, diagonal QS = 8 cm.
figure: Rectangle PQRS, P bottom-left, Q bottom-right, R top-right, S top-left; PQ = 4 cm; diagonal QS = 8 cm; right angles at P and Q.
note: Other side sqrt(64 − 16) = sqrt(48), about 6.9 cm (computed check).

question: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 3 cm and the diagonal is of length 7 cm.
answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = DC = 3 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm. The other sides AD = BC are about 6.3 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 3 cm.
At A draw a perpendicular line.
With the compass opened to 7 cm and centre B, draw an arc cutting this perpendicular at D (BD = 7 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to AB at B and a line through D perpendicular to AD. They meet at C.
Check: AB = DC = 3 cm, AD = BC, angles 90°, diagonal BD = 7 cm.
figure: Rectangle ABCD, A bottom-left, B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left; AB = 3 cm; diagonal BD = 7 cm; right angles at A and B.
note: Other side sqrt(49 − 9) = sqrt(40), about 6.3 cm (computed check).

question: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm. The house has a rectangular part with base DE = 5 cm and vertical sides DB = 5 cm and EC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, a roof with sides AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm meeting at the top point A, and a curved arc from B to C.
answer: A house with DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, apex A found as the point 5 cm from both B and C, and an arc from B to C drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. Since BC = 5 cm as well, triangle ABC has all sides 5 cm.
steps: Draw base DE = 5 cm. Draw perpendiculars at D and E and mark B and C each 5 cm up. Draw the door, 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall, on DE.
To find A, which is 5 cm from both B and C: set the compass to 5 cm and draw an arc from B (the circle of all points 5 cm from B).
With the same 5 cm opening draw an arc from C. The two arcs meet at A, which is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C. Join AB and AC.
With the compass at A and radius 5 cm, draw the arc from B to C (it bulges down into the house).
Check AB = AC = 5 cm.
figure: House: DE = 5 cm base (D left, E right); DB and EC vertical, each 5 cm; door of width 1 cm and height 2 cm standing on DE; A above, AB = AC = 5 cm; arc BC centred at A with radius 5 cm, bulging downward.

question: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at a point (the apex A). How far is that point from B? How far is it from C?
answer: a) 5 cm, b) 5 cm. So it is the point A.
steps: The point lies on the circle centred at B with radius 5 cm.
So it is 5 cm from B.
It also lies on the circle centred at C with radius 5 cm, so it is 5 cm from C.
This is the apex A.
figure: Two circles of radius 5 cm, centred at B and C with BC = 5 cm, crossing each other above the line BC.
note: Follows from the definition of a circle.

question: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A?
answer: No. Only a part of each circle is needed, so short arcs of radius 5 cm from B and from C that cross at A are enough.
steps: The point A is where the two circles cross.
Only the small parts near the crossing matter.
Draw just arcs from B and from C with 5 cm radius.
Where they cross is A.
note: Answer stated in the book text.

question: Construct a bigger house in which all the sides are of length 7 cm.
answer: A house like the earlier one with all border lines 7 cm: DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 7 cm, apex A 7 cm from B and from C, and an arc BC with centre A and radius 7 cm. The book's solution draws a door 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall.
steps: Draw DE = 7 cm, then perpendiculars at D and E; mark B and C 7 cm above D and E.
Draw a door on DE (the book's solution uses 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall).
With the compass at 7 cm, draw arcs from B and from C. They meet at A. Join AB and AC.
With the compass at A and radius 7 cm, draw the arc from B to C.
Check: every border line is 7 cm.
figure: House: DE = 7 cm, DB = 7 cm, EC = 7 cm, AB = 7 cm, AC = 7 cm, door 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall on the base, arc from B to C bulging downward.
note: The question only fixes the border lines at 7 cm; the door size of 2 cm by 3 cm is from the book's solution figure.

question: Try to recreate ‘A Person’, ‘Wavy Wave’, and ‘Eyes’ from the section ‘Artwork’, using ideas involved in the ‘House’ construction.
answer: Open drawing. A correct drawing shows: A Person (a circle for the head, for example radius 2 cm, a short neck line, and a 4 cm by 4 cm square body in the book's solution); Wavy Wave (equal half circles drawn alternately above and below a central line); Eyes (two matching lens-shaped eyes, each made from an upper and a lower arc drawn from compass points A above and B below, placed symmetrically, with a filled round pupil).
steps: Person: draw a circle with the compass for the head, then a neck line and a square for the body.
Wave: mark equal parts on a central line and draw half circles with the compass, one above and the next below.
Eyes: draw a light horizontal line. From a point A above it draw the lower curve, and from a point B below it draw the upper curve, with the same compass opening, so the two arcs meet at the ends.
Place A and B symmetrically (same distance from the line) so the eye is symmetrical.
Copy the eye for the second one and add the pupils.
figure: Book solution: a person made of a circle of radius 2 cm on a neck line above a square of side 4 cm; a wave of two shaded half-circle bumps, one above and one below a central line; two lens-shaped eyes side by side each with a filled round pupil.
note: Hint A (Eyes) says the placement of points A and B must be estimated so the upper and lower curves are symmetric.

question: Is there a 4-sided figure in which all the sides are equal in length but is not a square? If such a figure exists, can you construct it?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Does such a figure exist?
parts.answer: Yes, for example a rhombus (a slanted square).

parts.label: b
parts.question: Can you construct it?
parts.answer: Yes, using arcs from two points that are 5 cm from the common vertex.

answer: a) Yes, a rhombus (diamond) with four equal sides and angles that are not 90°; b) yes, it can be constructed with compass arcs.
steps: Take side length 5 cm. Draw AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm with angle A not equal to 90°, for example 60°.
The fourth point D must be 5 cm from both B and C.
With the compass at 5 cm, draw an arc from B and an arc from C. They cross at D.
Join BD and CD. All four sides AB, AC, BD, CD are 5 cm.
The angles are not 90°, so it is not a square.
figure: Book solution: a rhombus (diamond shape) with four equal sides, drawn without measurements. Hint figure: angle with vertex A, AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm.
note: Book solution figure shows a rhombus with no measurements; its proportions look like angles 60° and 120°, but this is not stated. Any angle at A other than 90° works.
